rules.rule:
User interface. The built-in TypeScript rules already cover hook misuse, render side effects,
over-memoisation and inline styles — this is only what they do not.

## Accessibility — review is the only guard here

There is no accessibility linter in this project and around fifty files write `aria` attributes by
hand.

- Flag a `div` or `span` with `onClick`: a native `button` is almost always the fix, rather than
  adding role, `tabIndex` and a key handler.
- Flag an input without a programmatic label, an icon-only control without an accessible name, and
  an image without `alt` (empty `alt` for decoration, stated explicitly).
- Flag a dialog or menu that does not trap focus and restore it on close.
- Flag state conveyed by colour alone, and `aria-*` duplicating native semantics — wrong ARIA is
  worse than none.

## Reuse before building

Around eighty shared components already exist in `shared/ui` — button, card, modal, popover,
confirm dialog, data table header, avatar, action menu. A screen that hand-rolls one looks almost
right and behaves differently under a keyboard.

- Check `shared/ui` before accepting a new component; if a close match exists, name it and prefer a
  prop over a second implementation.
- Flag a hand-built dialog, dropdown, tooltip or tab strip where a shared one exists.
- Flag a plainly generic component added to a feature folder, and a feature-specific concern pushed
  into `shared/ui`.

## Tokens, not literals

Ratchet tests already enforce raw hex, the type scale and the brand palette; be consistent with
them.

- Flag a literal colour, an off-scale font size or spacing value, and a hardcoded breakpoint,
  radius, shadow or z-index — competing z-index values cause layering bugs that appear only once
  both components are on screen.

## Consistency and failure states

- The same action needs the same word everywhere: flag `Delete` beside an equivalent `Remove`.
- An empty result and a failed request must not render the same thing — one says there is nothing,
  the other that we do not know.
- Flag an async view with no loading and error state, a destructive action with no confirmation,
  and a form that can be submitted twice.
- Flag a user-facing string written literally in a component: this app has locale files. Flag a
  sentence built by concatenation — word order differs between languages.
